planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter or set out nursery plants after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil; established plants tolerate heat and drought once rooted in.

directions: Whorled clary sends up branching, slightly sticky stems lined with heart-shaped, crinkled basal leaves, topped from early to late summer by long, loose spikes where the small lilac-purple flowers appear in distinct, tiered whorls that give the plant its common name. It is tougher and more heat-tolerant than many of its showier sage relatives, shrugging off poor, dry, alkaline soils that would set back lusher perennials, and it attracts a steady stream of bees throughout its long bloom season. Shear the spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a second round of bloom into fall, and avoid rich, overly moist soil, which causes lax, floppy growth. Plants are short-lived in humid climates but self-sow readily, keeping a patch going for years.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps spread readily and can be divided every two to three years.

directions: Hungarian speedwell forms a spreading clump of deeply cut, toothed foliage topped in late spring to early summer by dense, upright racemes of gentian-blue, four-lobed flowers that make an eye-catching show at the front of a sunny border or rock garden. It is one of the parent species behind many of the compact blue-flowered garden speedwells sold under cultivar names, but the species itself is a vigorous, reliable grower in its own right. Deadhead the spent spikes to tidy the clump and occasionally coax a lighter second bloom, and divide congested plants in spring or fall to maintain good vigor and airflow. It tolerates poor, rocky soils and light drought once established, making it a dependable choice for sunny slopes and gravel gardens.

planting.note: Set out rooted divisions or plugs in spring into well-drained soil; the creeping stems root as they spread, so space plants to allow the mat to knit together within a season or two.

directions: Caucasian speedwell forms a tight, low mat of small, bronze-tinged green leaves that hugs the ground and roots along its creeping stems, making it a useful edging plant or filler between stepping stones. In mid to late spring it produces a dense flush of small, saucer-shaped blue flowers with a pale center held just above the foliage, covering the mat so thoroughly that little leaf shows through at peak bloom. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and resents soggy winter conditions, which can cause the dense foliage to rot. Shear lightly after flowering to keep growth compact and encourage fresh foliage for the rest of the season.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter or set out nursery plants after the last frost into lean, fast-draining soil; this species tolerates more summer humidity and heavier soils than many Western penstemons.

directions: Native to the mountains of Mexico and Guatemala, Gulf Coast penstemon sends up slender, branching stems lined with narrow, toothed leaves and topped from late spring through fall with loose spikes of tubular, bell-shaped flowers ranging from violet-purple to rose-pink. It is notably more tolerant of summer humidity and garden soils than many western penstemon species, which makes it a reliable long-blooming choice for southern and southwestern perennial borders. Deadhead spent spikes to extend the long bloom season, and grow in sharply drained soil since wet feet in winter are its biggest threat. Hummingbirds visit the flowers steadily throughout the growing season.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter or set divisions out after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants shrug off summer drought.

directions: Wand sage produces a basal rosette of wrinkled, gray-green leaves from which slender, wand-like flowering stems rise in early to midsummer, branching near the top into airy spikes of small violet-blue flowers set against burgundy-tinted calyces that remain attractive even as the blooms fade. Native to dry, rocky slopes across the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia, it is well suited to gravel gardens and sunny borders with sharp drainage, where it resents winter wet far more than cold. Cut the flowering stems back after bloom to tidy the clump and may encourage sporadic rebloom later in the season. It combines well with other dryland perennials such as catmint and lavender, needing little supplemental water once established.
